text: Chaos engineering has an unfortunate name, because it sounds like mischief — randomly breaking things in production and seeing what happens. That is not what the discipline actually is. It is a controlled, hypothesis-driven way of testing whether a system's real resilience matches what the team believes about it, and it is the subject of this entire chapter.

A real chaos experiment always follows the same four-part structure. First, define steady state: a specific, measurable signal for normal behavior, like checkout success rate staying at or above 99.9 percent. Second, form a hypothesis — a falsifiable claim about how the system should respond to one specific failure. Third, inject that failure for real: kill a pod, add network latency, black out a dependency. Fourth, compare the result to the hypothesis and see whether steady state actually held.

Here's what a usable hypothesis actually looks like written down: steady state is checkout success rate at or above 99.9 percent, the injected failure is terminating one of three payment-service pods, and the expected result is that success rate holds because traffic reroutes to the remaining two. If it holds, the team's belief about resilience is now backed by evidence. If it drops, they've found a real weakness safely, with people watching, instead of during an actual outage.

This practice traces back to Netflix in the early 2010s. As the company migrated to AWS, engineers built Chaos Monkey, a tool that randomly terminated production instances — deliberately, on a Tuesday afternoon, with the team watching, rather than leaving that discovery to an unplanned outage at 3 a.m. Chaos Monkey was later open-sourced as part of Netflix's Simian Army, and it's the historical root of the much broader practice this chapter covers.

That's what chaos engineering actually tests for: not whether one unit of code works in isolation, but whether the system's real behavior under a real failure matches what the team believes. Next lesson turns this into practice — the safety discipline that makes it responsible to run a chaos experiment at all, including blast radius, kill switches, and abort criteria defined before anything gets touched.
